<!-- P1: what is the question of this section -->

<!-- SUPERSEDED (incentive RAP, 2026-09-24):
Firms are known to overreport costs when tax enforcement tightens, but because governments seldom change rates in ways researchers can exploit, less is known about whether firms also overreport more when tax rates rise. I address this question in this chapter. After Colombia raised the sales-tax rate on most manufacturing industries in 1983, I find that unincorporated firms overreported more of their inputs, and by 1987 overreporting had reached about 8% of true materials.
-->

Firms are known to overreport costs when tax enforcement tightens, which raises the expected cost of evading, but less is known about the benefit side: whether they overreport more when the tax rate, which sets how much each peso of fictitious inputs saves, goes up. I investigate this question and find evidence that input overreporting rises when the tax rate increases. In 1983, Colombia raised the sales-tax rate in most manufacturing industries while others remained exempt. <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): Overreporting by unincorporated firms escalated after the reform, reaching about 8% of true materials by 1987, and the increase was concentrated in the industries where the net incentives increase the most. --> Overreporting by unincorporated firms rose after the reform, reaching about 8% of true materials by 1987, and the increase was concentrated in the industries where the rate went up.

<!-- P2: why does this matter? -->

Whether firms evade more when tax rates rise matters for policymakers. If evasion rises with the rate, a tax increase raises less revenue than its mechanical effect suggests, and evasion affects the marginal efficiency cost of raising tax rates [@Slemrod2019, p. 907]. The concern is especially relevant for sales and value-added taxes, whose credit on purchases is a natural target of fictitious deductions [@Carrillo2022]. Yet recent empirical work says more about enforcement than about tax rates.

The 1983 reform changed statutory rates rather than enforcement, which makes it a rare setting in which to study this question. Governments have agreed to randomize letters, audits and information reporting, but not tax rates [@Slemrod2019], and among the studies Slemrod reviews, the evidence on tax rates comes mostly from misreported imports [@FismanWei2004; @HandleyMoore2017]. The same literature shows that firms adjust reported costs: <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): when tax authorities forced firms --> when tax authorities pushed firms to report more revenue, Ecuadorian firms raised reported costs by 96 and Armenian firms 70–80 cents per dollar of additional revenue [@Carrillo2017; @Asatryan2017]. <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24) (repeats P1 and P2): Because these studies vary enforcement, less is known about whether input overreporting also responds to tax rates. --> <!-- SUPERSEDED (RAP revision, 2026-09-24): The 1983 reform, a statutory change in tax rates, lets me study this question. -->

<!-- P4 (moved): how does this tie to the model -->

In the model, the sales tax rate shifts the marginal benefit of overreporting materials: a higher $\tau$ raises the credit claimed on each peso of fictitious inputs (@sec-model). Although the model has no income tax, the same logic extends to it: overreported inputs also lower reported profits and, thus, the income-tax base. An increase in either rate therefore raises the incentive to overreport inputs, and a decrease lowers it.

<!-- P3: what does the reform do to firms -->

The 1983 fiscal policy changed incentives *across* industries and *within* industries. Across industries, the sales tax rate increased from 6% to 10% for most ST-liable industries, while ST-exempt industries remained exempt. Within industries, the income tax changed by juridical organization (JO), and in the opposite direction. *Ley 9 de 1983* cut individual income-tax rates by 4.6 percentage points on average across income brackets relative to the 1982 schedule, and thus proprietorships faced lower rates [@PerryCardenas1986]. LLCs received a smaller cut, from 20% to 18% [@PerryCardenas1986]. Overreporting inputs lowers both taxes, through a larger credit on purchases and a smaller income-tax base, so the two changes pull the incentive to overreport in opposite directions. In ST-liable industries, the net incentive is therefore ambiguous for both: proprietorships were compensated for much of the sales-tax increase through the income tax, while LLCs were insufficiently compensated. In ST-exempt industries, the income-tax cut alone lowered the incentive for proprietorships and changed it little for LLCs, whose cut was small.

<!-- P5: who the groups are (incentive RAP, 2026-09-24) -->

Because the income-tax cut differed between proprietorships and LLCs, the reform's incentives also varied along the size distribution. Proprietorships have a single owner and are the smallest. <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): Governments find proprietorships harder to penetrate and where it is traditionally believed that evasion is persisten and more sustainable [@Slemrom2019]. --> Tax authorities find sole proprietorships and small businesses hard to penetrate, and evasion in them is more sustainable [@Slemrod2019, p. 940]. At the median, LLCs have about two and a half times proprietorships' labour and three times their gross output. LLCs have several owners and non-tradable shares. <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): Evidence from Spain suggests firms close to the auditing-threshold for the largest firms (in other words, larget than the micro firms) misreport significantly to escape scrutiny. --> In Spain, firms bunch just below the revenue threshold above which the Large Taxpayers' Unit monitors them more closely [@Almunia2018; @Slemrod2019, pp. 925–926]. At the top, corporations are several times larger than LLCs in capital, labour and gross output, and their shares are tradable. In addition, <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): the government holds corporations under close observation requiring a mandatory auditor at place. --> the government keeps corporations under close supervision and requires them to have an auditor. Lastly, since evidence suggests stock prices of public companies fall when news of their involvement in tax shelters becomes public [@HanlonSlemrod2009; @Slemrod2019, p. 909], corporations might have lower incentives to evade. In this chapter corporations serve as the benchmark of non-evaders, on the assumption that audited statements, third-party reporting and the market's reaction keep them from overreporting.

## Empirical approach {#sec-fiscal-approach}

From the materials FOC, for corporations, the truth-reporters, $i$ in industry $j$ at year $t$, the log share of materials' cost over sales is

$$
s_{ijt}^{C} = \ln\beta_j-\varepsilon_{ijt}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-corp}

where $s_{ijt}\equiv\ln(\rho_tM^*_{ijt}/P_tY_{ijt})$ is the log share of materials' cost over sales, $\beta_j$ is the output elasticity of materials of industry $j$, and $\varepsilon_{ijt}$ is the error term. For unincorporated firms, the evaders,

$$
s_{ijt}^{N} = \ln\beta_j + u_{ijt} - \varepsilon_{ijt}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-unincorp}

where $u_{ijt}=\ln(1+e_{ijt}/M_{ijt})$ is the overreporting of materials' cost due to tax evasion.

Let $D_{ijt}^N$ be a dummy indicating whether the firm is an unincorporated firm. Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}
  (1-D_{ijt}^N)s_{ijt} + D_{ijt}^N s_{ijt} =& (1-D_{ijt}^N)(\ln\beta_j-\varepsilon_{ijt}) + D_{ijt}^N \big(\ln\beta_j+u_{ijt}  - \varepsilon_{ijt}\big) \\
    s_{ijt} =& \ln\beta_j + D_{ijt}^N  u_{ijt} - \varepsilon_{ijt}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-stack}

Taking expectations,

$$
E[s_{ijt}|D^{N}=0,j]=\ln\beta_j, \qquad E[s_{ijt}|D^{N}=1,j]-E[s_{ijt}|D^{N}=0,j]= \mu
$$ {#eq-fiscal-mean}

identifies the average overreporting level, $\mu\equiv E[u_{ijt}\mid D^N_{ijt}=1]$, a population expectation; its estimate is $\hat\mu$.


In the case of the fiscal policy changes, I am interested in the changes in average tax evasion after the 1983 fiscal reform. Taking the difference of the expectations between year $t'$ and $t=1983$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
    s_{ijt'} - s_{ij,1983}
     &= D_{ijt}^N  (u_{ijt'} - u_{ij,1983}) - (\varepsilon_{ijt'} - \varepsilon_{ij,1983}) \\
    E[s_{ijt'}-s_{ij,1983}|D^{N}=1] &= \mu_{t'} - \mu_{1983} \equiv \Delta\mu_{t'}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-diff}

where $\mu_t$ is the annual average tax evasion of year $t$, and $\Delta\mu_{t}$ is the change in average tax evasion between year $t$ and 1983, the last full year before the reform took effect (@sec-setting-st).


The identifying assumptions are explicit in @eq-fiscal-stack and @eq-fiscal-diff: (i) corporations do not overreport (@eq-fiscal-corp); (ii) firms within an industry share a common Cobb-Douglas technology, with a constant output elasticity of materials $\beta_j$ (@eq-fiscal-corp and @eq-fiscal-unincorp); and (iii) the ex-post shock $\varepsilon_{ijt}$ is independent of evasion, true materials and juridical organization, with $E[\varepsilon_{ijt}\mid D^N_{ijt},t]=0$. 

<!-- Under (i)–(iii), in every year $t$,

$$
E[s_{ijt}\mid D^N_{ijt}=0,j,t]=\ln\beta_j,\qquad E[s_{ijt}\mid D^N_{ijt}=1,j,t]=\ln\beta_j+\mu_t .
$$ {#eq-fiscal-ident}

 -->


Even though @eq-fiscal-diff resembles a traditional difference-in-differences design, the result does not require parallel trends for identification. Under (i)-(iii), @eq-fiscal-stack and @eq-fiscal-diff show that the difference between unincorporated firms and corporations in year $t$ is the average overreporting itself, $\mu_t$, and changes in $\mu_t$ over time, including before 1983, are changes in evasion.

<!-- Compare this with a difference-in-differences design. There, each group's outcome carries its own time effect, $E[s_{ijt}\mid D^N_{ijt}=d,j,t]=\ln\beta_j+\lambda^d_t+d\,\mu_t$ for $d\in\{0,1\}$, and $\Delta\mu_t$ is identified only if the two time effects move together, $\lambda^1_t-\lambda^1_{1983}=\lambda^0_t-\lambda^0_{1983}$: parallel trends. The model has no such time effect. The materials FOC pins down a truth-reporting firm's log share at $\ln\beta_j-\varepsilon_{ijt}$, whatever happens to prices, demand or productivity, so $\lambda^0_t=\lambda^1_t=0$ follows from (ii) rather than being assumed. The difference between unincorporated firms and corporations in year $t$ is therefore not a comparison with a control group; it is average overreporting itself, $\mu_t$, and parallel trends is never invoked. Movements in $\mu_t$ before 1983 are changes in evasion, not violations of an identifying assumption. -->


To estimate @eq-fiscal-stack, I use the following regression specification,

$$
    s_{ijt} = \ln\beta_j + \sum_{t=1981}^{1991} \mu_t\, D_{ijt}^N\,\mathbb 1[\text{year}=t] + \zeta_{ijt}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-lvl-reg}

where $\mu_{t}$ is the average tax evasion of unincorporated firms in year $t$; $\ln\beta_j$ enter as industry fixed effects, estimated jointly with the $\mu_t$, so no first-stage estimate enters the regression and its standard errors need no bootstrap or generated-regressor correction; and $\zeta_{ijt}=\nu_{ijt}-\varepsilon_{ijt}$, where $u_{ijt} = \mu_t + \nu_{ijt}$ and $\nu_{ijt}$ is the idiosyncratic component of tax evasion that is not captured by the year dummies. Likewise, I estimate @eq-fiscal-diff with the following regression,

$$
    s_{ijt} = \ln\beta_j + \mu\, D_{ijt}^N+\sum_{t=1981}^{1991} \mathbb{1}[t\neq1983]\,\Delta\mu_t\, D_{ijt}^N\,\mathbb 1[\text{year}=t] + \zeta_{ijt}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-diff-reg}

where $\Delta\mu_{t}$ is the difference in tax evasion of unincorporated firms between year $t$ and 1983, the last full year before the reform took effect, and $\mu$ is the average tax evasion of unincorporated firms in 1983.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
**Draft note:** your "not a DiD" framing is now written up after @eq-fiscal-diff (identifying assumptions (i)–(iii)).

**Draft note (implementation):** the text now matches the code: log materials share as the outcome, with industry fixed effects ($\ln\beta_j$), two-way clustered by plant and year (`921.1-DD.R`, `921.2-het-slides.R`). $\mathcal V$ is used as the outcome only in the size-heterogeneity analysis.
:::

The 1983 fiscal reform changed incentives to evade taxes over time *differently* for firms in ST-liable and ST-exempt industries. Most ST-liable industries faced an ST rate *increase* from 6% to 10%, while ST-exempt industries *remained exempt* before and after the reform. Note that firms in *all* industries are subject to the income tax, which also generates incentives to evade taxes by overreporting input costs: lower reported profits due to higher input costs reduce the tax base, and thus the tax liability. Therefore, the income tax and the ST generate tax evasion incentives for firms in ST-liable industries, while only the income tax does for firms in ST-exempt industries. For unincorporated firms,

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_{ijt}^{N} &= \ln\beta_j + u^{ST}_{ijt} + u^{IT}_{ijt}-\varepsilon_{ijt} & j &\in \text{ST-Liable} \\
s_{ijt}^{N} &= \ln\beta_j + u^{IT}_{ijt}-\varepsilon_{ijt} & j &\in \text{ST-Exempt}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-noncorp}

where $u^{ST}_{ijt}$ and $u^{IT}_{ijt}$ stand for the overreporting due to the ST and the income tax (IT), respectively. Let $D^E_{ijt}$ be a dummy indicating whether the industry is ST-exempt and $D^{L}_{ijt}$ a dummy indicating whether the industry is ST-liable, such that $D^E_{ijt} + D^{L}_{ijt} = 1$. Combining @eq-fiscal-corp with @eq-fiscal-noncorp,

$$
    s_{ijt} = \ln\beta_j + D_{ijt}^N D^E_{ijt}\, u^{IT}_{ijt} + D_{ijt}^N D^{L}_{ijt} (u^{ST}_{ijt} + u^{IT}_{ijt}) - \varepsilon_{ijt}
$$ {#eq-fiscal-lvl-split}

Taking expectations,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[s_{ijt}|D^{N}=1,D^E=1,j]-\ln\beta_j &= \mu^{IT}_E \\
E[s_{ijt}|D^{N}=1,D^{L}=1,j]-\ln\beta_j &= \mu^{ST}_{L}+\mu^{IT}_{L}\equiv\mu^{ST+IT}_{L}
\end{aligned}
$$

identifies the average overreporting by firms in ST-exempt industries, $\mu^{IT}_E$, and in ST-liable industries, $\mu^{ST+IT}_{L}$. If I assume $\mu^{IT}_E = \mu^{IT}_{L}$, I can also identify the overreporting due to ST, $\mu^{ST}_{L}$. Since income-tax rates depend on the juridical organization and not on the industry, I assume that the income tax generates the same incentives to evade taxes across industries, whether they are exempt of ST or not. Because I aggregate different juridical organizations in exempt and liable industries into unincorporated firms, this assumption might break if the composition of juridical organizations is non-trivially different between exempt and liable industries. The regression versions of @eq-fiscal-lvl-reg and @eq-fiscal-diff-reg interact the year dummies with $D^N_{ijt}D^E_{ijt}$ and $D^N_{ijt}D^L_{ijt}$, giving one path per industry type, $\mu_{E,t}$ and $\mu_{L,t}$ (and $\Delta\mu_{E,t}$, $\Delta\mu_{L,t}$ relative to 1983). Splitting unincorporated firms further by JO, into LLCs and proprietorships, gives four such paths.

### Changes in true materials cannot explain the pattern {#sec-fiscal-m}

Since $u_{ijt}=\ln(1+e_{ijt}/M_{ijt})$, the empirical exercise remains valid as long as changes in $s$ are not explained by changes in $M$ (or $\varepsilon$), but only by $e$ or $e/M$: changes in the proxy should be explained by changes to the incentives to adjust overreporting, not by firms adjusting their optimal choice of true inputs.

The alternative argument is that changes in true inputs explain the increase in the overreporting share. Suppose $e$ is unchanged. Then, after the reform, unincorporated firms would have to lower their true inputs, by either an increase in relative prices or productivity shocks. Productivity shocks are unrelated to tax rates, so this is unlikely. According to the FOC, taxes do not show in the optimal choice of firms. Besides, the increase after the reform is gradual, while the reform made only a one-time change. So this alternative argument does not hold. The evasion channel is more direct: an increase in the sales tax rate leads to an increase in the overreporting share because a higher tax rate increases the marginal benefit of overreporting.

<!-- SUPERSEDED (incentive RAP, 2026-09-24): After the fiscal reform of 1983 increased the sales tax rate, tax evasion through input overreporting increased gradually (@fig-fiscal-all, @tbl-fiscal-all). --> Overreporting rose once the reform raised the benefit of overreporting in most industries: after the sales-tax increase took effect, input overreporting by unincorporated firms increased gradually (@fig-fiscal-all, @tbl-fiscal-all). Input overreporting reached an average of 8% in 1987, where it stabilized until 1990.

The standard errors of the levels and of the differences over time look very different. In levels, the large standard errors suggest that tax evasion is widely heterogeneous across firms. This heterogeneity may come from differences in the tax rate due to firm characteristics (industry, JO, and exports), <!--in the (perceived) probability of detection (the model assumes risk neutrality, but firms might have different perceived probabilities),--> and in the cost of evasion across firms. The differences over time, however, are tight for a mechanical reason. Every year's level $\hat\mu_t$ is estimated against the same baseline, so estimation error in that baseline enters every year with the same sign, and the level estimates are strongly positively correlated. Since $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_t-\hat\mu_{1983})=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_t)+\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_{1983})-2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\mu_t,\hat\mu_{1983})$, this shared error cancels in the differences. The correlation affects inference only, not the consistency of the estimates: the regressors are group-by-year dummies, and $E[\zeta_{ijt}\mid D^N_{ijt},\text{year}]=0$ because $\varepsilon$ is independent of $(e,M)$ and $\nu_{ijt}$ is, by construction, the deviation from the group-year mean. Standard errors are two-way clustered by plant and year.

- Salvador reframed this in a meeting; the mechanical (covariance) explanation above replaces the old "heterogeneity is constant over time" reading from the slides.
- Only 11 year clusters: two-way cluster-robust SEs are unreliable with so few clusters. Robustness: wild cluster bootstrap by year, or cluster by plant only.
- Composition: $\mu_t$ is a cross-sectional mean, so entry, exit, and switches in juridical organization (e.g. LLCs incorporating after the 1986 unification of the entity-level income tax) can move it. Robustness: add plant fixed effects (within-firm changes).
:::

### Overreporting before the reform {#sec-fiscal-pre}

Corporations are a clean comparison group that will not react to the policy changes, because the assumption is that these firms do not evade taxes by overreporting. Thus, I can interpret the estimates as the change in overreporting relative to 1983, the last full year before the reform took effect.

The policy changes of the time were the result of a public debate following the 1981 report of the Bird–Wiesner Mission, a technical mission on Colombia's intergovernmental finances led by Richard Bird (international tax expert) and Eduardo Wiesner (Colombian economist) that recommended better tax administration to reduce evasion [@JunguitoRincon2004; @Bolanos2019]. The reform was enacted at the end of December 1983 and took effect on 1 April 1984 (@sec-setting-st). These changes aimed to reduce the fiscal deficit without resorting to money financing and to reactivate investment through tax incentives, while broadening the tax base and simplifying collection [@Sanchez1994].

A plausible scenario is that firms could have reduced their overreporting during the public debate as a way to signal compliance and avoid further tax increases, and then reverted their behaviour after the reform was enacted. If this is the case, then part of the increase in overreporting after 1983 is a return to previous levels of tax evasion. More data points before 1981 would help to clarify this issue.

:::

The increase is concentrated where the sales tax, and with it the benefit of overreporting, went up. After the fiscal reform of 1983, unincorporated firms in ST-liable industries increased tax evasion significantly, while those in ST-exempt industries increased it only slightly (@fig-fiscal-liable, @tbl-fiscal-liable). In ST-liable industries, overreporting rose gradually until 1987 and stabilized until 1990. In ST-exempt industries, the increase was moderate, with a second rise between 1987 and 1990. The increase is *larger* for ST-liable firms, the most affected by the reform.

<!-- SUPERSEDED (incentive RAP, 2026-09-24): The comparison lines up with the incentives described at the start of this chapter. --> This comparison isolates the sales tax as a shifter of the marginal benefit: ST-liable industries faced the rate increase, while ST-exempt industries did not. Firms in ST-liable industries faced a higher sales tax, only partly offset by lower income-tax rates, while firms in ST-exempt industries faced the income-tax cut alone. The larger response in ST-liable industries is consistent with the sales-tax increase dominating. The slight increase in ST-exempt industries, driven by proprietorships, is unexpected; @sec-fiscal-jo discusses two possible explanations.

<!-- SUPERSEDED (incentive RAP, 2026-09-24): Results: LLCs vs. proprietorships {#sec-fiscal-jo} -->
## Results: income-tax incentives, LLCs vs. proprietorships {#sec-fiscal-jo}

![Overreporting of LLCs relative to corporations by year, 1981–1991, in ST-exempt and ST-liable industries. Points are coefficient estimates with 95% confidence intervals; standard errors two-way clustered by plant and year; industry fixed effects. Left panel: levels, $\hat\mu_t$; right panel: differences with respect to 1983, $\Delta\hat\mu_t$. The dashed line marks 1983, the last full year before the reform took effect.](/figures/ch07-fiscal-llc.png){#fig-fiscal-llc}

:::{#tbl-fiscal-llc}
![](/tables/ch07-fiscal-llc.png)

Overreporting of LLCs in ST-exempt and ST-liable industries. Coefficients behind the figure, by year: levels ($\hat\mu_t$) and differences with respect to 1983 ($\Delta\hat\mu_t$).
:::

![Overreporting of proprietorships relative to corporations by year, 1981–1991, in ST-exempt and ST-liable industries. Points are coefficient estimates with 95% confidence intervals; standard errors two-way clustered by plant and year; industry fixed effects. Left panel: levels, $\hat\mu_t$; right panel: differences with respect to 1983, $\Delta\hat\mu_t$. The dashed line marks 1983, the last full year before the reform took effect.](/figures/ch07-fiscal-prt.png){#fig-fiscal-prt}

:::{#tbl-fiscal-prt}
![](/tables/ch07-fiscal-prt.png)

Overreporting of proprietorships in ST-exempt and ST-liable industries. Coefficients behind the figure, by year: levels ($\hat\mu_t$) and differences with respect to 1983 ($\Delta\hat\mu_t$).
:::

Within industries, the income-tax cut lowered the benefit of overreporting, by more for proprietorships than for LLCs. LLCs in ST-liable industries show a significant increase in tax evasion, <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): while LLCs in exempt industries show no significant change --> while LLCs in exempt industries show changes of about one percentage point or less (@fig-fiscal-llc, @tbl-fiscal-llc). LLCs in exempt industries mainly faced a decrease in their entity-level income tax. This decrease would lead to lower incentives to evade taxes. However, since the reduction is small, <!-- SUPERSEDED (claims check, 2026-09-24): it is not unreasonable to find no evidence of significant changes in tax evasion for these industries. --> it is not unreasonable to find only small changes in tax evasion for these industries. In ST-liable industries, LLCs faced two opposing effects: the increase in sales tax rates, which would increase incentives to evade taxes, and the income-tax cut, which would decrease incentives to evade taxes. The evidence suggests that the increase in sales tax rates dominates the effect of the income-tax cut, leading to a significant increase in tax evasion for LLCs in ST-liable industries.

Proprietorships show a more heterogeneous response (@fig-fiscal-prt, @tbl-fiscal-prt). In ST-liable industries, their overreporting barely changed in 1984–1985, consistent with the income-tax cut compensating them for much of the sales-tax increase; it rose from 1986 onward, peaking in 1987–1988. In ST-exempt industries, their overreporting rose after 1983, even though they faced only the income-tax cut. This result is unexpected, and I offer two possible explanations. First, the incentive to overreport depends on the marginal tax rate, not the average one, and the 1983 cut in marginal rates was much smaller than the cut in average rates at both ends of the income distribution: close to zero at low incomes and about 2 percentage points at high incomes (@tbl-marg-tax-1983). Second, the 1982–1983 changes stopped individuals from fully deducting their financial expenses [@Ocampo1983], which gave proprietorships, but not LLCs, a reason to replace a lost deduction with overreported inputs.

Proprietorships' standard errors are also several times those of LLCs, which suggests that they responded less uniformly. This is plausible: proprietorships range from family workshops to young entrepreneurial firms, with varying degrees of process standardization, record-keeping, while LLCs tend to be larger firms with more established processes, and their responses look more homogeneous.

## Takeaways and link to the structural model {#sec-fiscal-takeaways}

<!-- SUPERSEDED (incentive RAP, 2026-09-24):
The 1983 reform offers empirical evidence that firms overreport inputs in response to tax incentives. Overreporting by unincorporated firms rose after the reform took effect, and it rose most where the net incentive rose most: in ST-liable industries, where the sales tax went up, and among LLCs, whose small income-tax cut did little to offset it. Proprietorships, compensated for much of the sales-tax increase by a larger income-tax cut, barely responded at first. The one result that does not fit, the rise among proprietorships in ST-exempt industries, has two possible explanations in the reform's other provisions (@sec-fiscal-jo).
-->

Input overreporting rises with the marginal benefit of overreporting. After the 1983 reform raised the sales tax, overreporting by unincorporated firms increased, reaching about 8% of true materials by 1987, and the increase was concentrated in ST-liable industries, where the benefit rose. Within those industries it rose most among LLCs, whose small income-tax cut left most of the sales-tax increase in place, while proprietorships, compensated by a larger income-tax cut, barely responded at first. The one result that does not fit, the rise among proprietorships in ST-exempt industries, has two possible explanations in the reform's other provisions (@sec-fiscal-jo).

This evidence supports the model's key comparative static, $\partial e^*/\partial\tau>0$ (@sec-model), which the structural estimation cannot test by regression: overreporting and the tax rate are both built from the same reported materials, so a regression of one on the other is mechanically biased. It also supports the identification of the detection probability in @sec-counterfactual, which rests on the same source of variation: changes in the sales-tax benefit of overreporting move evasion.
